transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-21
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Sophie Chen (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood Optimize), Lena Ortiz (ByteWave - Head of ML), Arjun Patel (ByteWave - CTO), Maya Singh (ByteWave - Platform)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8), demonstration of quality vs latency tradeoffs for ByteWave's summarization use case, discussion of pilot next steps and security/compliance asks. Some transcription artifacts, speaker overlaps.

Topics:
- INT8 vs FP8 profiles and when to pick each
- Quality regressions and how to monitor (eval sets, automated regs)
- Latency measurements and batching strategies (continuous batching, KV cache)
- Dedicated vs Hosted trade-offs for pilot
- Security: KMS, audit logs, data residency

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Park: Hey everyone, welcome thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off, this is the Optimize walkthrough, focus on quantization profiles INT8 and FP8 and how those trade quality for latency and cost for the summarization pipeline you mentioned in the prep notes.
[00:22] Lena Ortiz: Thanks Jamie, excited to see this. Quick context: our summarization runs at about ~60 RPS peak, about 2k tokens avg per request, and we care a lot about latency under 500ms p50 for interactive use.
[00:40] Sophie Chen: Great, thanks Lena, that helps — and do you have a breakdown of request size distribution? is it long tail?
[00:45] Maya Singh: Yeah it's a long tail, most are 1k–2.5k tokens, maybe 10% above 3k, so we do some truncation but quality matters for the high-tier customers.
[01:10] Marco Ruiz: Okay, so we'll demo two profiles: an INT8 profile optimized for cost and throughput, and an FP8 profile that preserves quality at slightly higher latency; we'll show perf numbers and quality deltas on your eval set.
[01:40] Arjun Patel: Quick Q — how stable are FP8 quant models across sequence length? our tail requests worry me.
[01:50] Sophie Chen: Good question. FP8 tends to preserve numeric range better so it can be more stable for long sequences, but it depends on the model's activation distributions; our Optimize engine will profile your traces and suggest kernel combos. sometimes FP8 gives better p99 but with higher cost.
[02:20] Lena Ortiz: And what about hallucination/precision on facts? we can't drop below a certain ROUGE/L or our customers will complain.
[02:30] Jamie Park: Right, we usually set a Q-threshold: baseline is FP16 full precision; then INT8 aimed for no more than X% quality drop on your evals — we measure with BLEU/ROUGE and a small hand-curated prompt set. We'll show numbers from your eval later in the call.
[03:05] [Slight crosstalk] Sophie Chen: I'm pulling up the dashboard — ok I'm sharing my screen — you should see the Optimize console: quant profiles, latency histograms, and the quality vs latency plot.
[03:30] [Screen share noise] Sophie Chen: Here is the first slide, base model: redwood-gpt-large (example), baseline FP16 p50 = 420ms, p95 = 780ms on GPU-x. INT8 profile reduced median to ~260ms but we saw a mean quality drop ~3.2% on your summarization eval set. FP8 median was ~330ms with quality drop ~0.8%.
[04:05] Lena Ortiz: So INT8 gives us near 2x median improvement but a non-trivial quality drop, FP8 seems like a nice middle ground. Those numbers assume continuous batching?
[04:20] Marco Ruiz: Yes those include continuous batching at 128ms window and prefix KV cache enabled for conversational contexts. For single-turn summarization the cache helps across repeated tokens for similar prompts.
[04:50] Arjun Patel: How deterministic are these numbers? I mean with real traffic we'll see variance, right?
[05:00] Sophie Chen: Absolutely, the console shows distributions plus confidence intervals; we can run bench jobs with a replay of your sampled traffic to get tighter estimates. We recommend a pilot with Dedicated to remove noisy multi-tenant variance.
[05:30] Lena Ortiz: For pilot we'd want to test at our 60 RPS workload, can Redwood provision dedicated capacity for that?
[05:38] Jamie Park: Yes we can size a Dedicated pool for that envelope — we'll propose a config. Also, we can run a compare test: baseline FP16 vs INT8 vs FP8 using your eval set and a traffic replay.
[06:05] Maya Singh: On security, how do keys and logs work if we go Dedicated? we need KMS and audit logs in our VPC.
[06:15] Jamie Park: For Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS and we can push logs to your SIEM. Audit logs and RBAC are available; I'll send the security pack after the call.
[06:40] [Pause while screen shows quality plots]
[07:10] Sophie Chen: Back to the quality tradeoffs — here's a scatter: x-axis is median latency, y-axis is relative quality (higher is better). Each dot is a profile: FP16 baseline at top-right, INT8 lower-right (fast but lower quality), FP8 near top-middle. We also overlay cost per 1M tokens.
[07:40] Lena Ortiz: Those cost numbers are helpful; can you quantify cost delta? we have a hard budget for inference spend.
[07:50] Marco Ruiz: INT8 typically reduces unit cost by ~40–50% vs FP16; FP8 is around 20–30% savings depending on kernels and hardware. But because INT8 might require more beam checks or reruns for quality, effective cost can be higher if you have to do safety re-runs — so we look at end-to-end quality-adjusted cost.
[08:20] Arjun Patel: How do you measure quality-adjusted cost? is that a Redwood metric?
[08:28] Sophie Chen: It's a simple metric we compute: cost_per_request / (1 - quality_regression_rate) where quality_regression_rate is measured on critical eval prompts. We can customize that to your SLAs.
[08:55] [Screen zoom on calibration plots]
[09:30] Sophie Chen: Now I'll demo a live inference run from your eval set. First FP16 baseline: you can see references vs model output, BLEU/ROUGE. Next INT8: small wording changes, ROUGE down 2.9% on average, some edge cases show more divergence. FP8: mostly intact with 0.7% avg drop.
[10:20] Lena Ortiz: Do you have examples of failure modes? we need to see where INT8 breaks so we can build guard rails.
[10:30] Marco Ruiz: Yes — we'll attach a short list of prompts that produced the largest diffs. In our experience it's often numeric tables or long-tail tokens with very low probability mass.
[11:00] Arjun Patel: Can we do hybrid routing? e.g., route high-value customers to FP8 or FP16 and low-latency traffic to INT8?
[11:10] Jamie Park: Absolutely. Smart routing is a first-class pattern: route by customer tier, latency SLO, or confidence threshold. We can wire a classifier to the request and route accordingly; Redwood Optimize has traffic splitting and automatic fallback.
[11:40] Maya Singh: Is confidence threshold computed per-token or per-response?
[11:50] Sophie Chen: Typically per-response — we compute a scoring function from logits and calibration; if below threshold we can escalate to higher-precision model or run a quick re-rank.
[12:10] [Background typing noises]
[12:50] Sophie Chen: Back to perf — here's a p99 plot. INT8 p99 can be worse if quantization triggers kernel fallbacks; FP8 p99 is often more predictable. We add kernel selection heuristics to avoid regressions.
[13:20] Lena Ortiz: Do you maintain a model catalog mapping profiles to hardware? e.g., on A100 vs H100 differences?
[13:30] Marco Ruiz: Yes, catalog includes recommended profiles by GPU generation. H100 with FP8 kernels often gives better throughput/quality than older hardware. We'll provide a recommended config for your chosen Dedicated instance types.
[13:55] Arjun Patel: For the pilot, can we bring our own model or do we have to use Redwood-curated ones?
[14:03] Jamie Park: We support customer models in Dedicated/Private deployments; for hosted we can host customer models with additional review. For POCs it's common to run your checkpoint on Dedicated.
[14:30] Lena Ortiz: Ok good. About monitoring, how will we detect quality regressions post-rollout?
[14:38] Sophie Chen: We integrate evals into CI; you upload a prompt set and Redwood runs continuous checks. We also support drift detection and can alert on metrics like ROUGE drop > threshold or increased token divergence.
[15:05] [Interruption] Arjun Patel: Do you have SLO guards to automatically rollback?
[15:12] Marco Ruiz: Yes, rollouts can be canary with automatic rollback if key metrics cross thresholds. We support A/B and canary with traffic percentages and metric gating.
[15:45] Sophie Chen: Switching back to the console, here's the recommended INT8 profile we generated for your model: per-layer calibration, outlier clipping enabled, mixed-precision for attention kernels. This reduces memory and improves throughput.
[16:20] Lena Ortiz: Outlier clipping — any risk of clipping meaningful tokens?
[16:28] Sophie Chen: Rare, but we tune the clip threshold on your evals. We usually start conservative and then push more aggressive profiles during the pilot if quality is acceptable.
[16:55] [Short pause]
[17:15] Jamie Park: Pricing — rough numbers in the pricing sheet: Dedicated hourly + per-token unit cost that varies by profile. We'll send a tailored estimate after you share expected traffic and retention needs.
[17:40] Maya Singh: Data retention and logs — we need to ensure PII is redacted before logs leave VPC. Can Redwood integrate with our redaction pipeline?
[17:50] Jamie Park: Yes, you can integrate pre-processing for redaction in your pipeline; we also offer customer-side masking before tokens are sent. For audit you can set policy to not log request text.
[18:20] Lena Ortiz: For the pilot, we want to try three profiles: FP16 baseline, FP8 recommended, and INT8 aggressive, with traffic split 20/50/30. Can Redwood run that and collect quality metrics?
[18:30] Sophie Chen: Yep we can. We'll set up the experiment and produce a report with cost/quality/latency tradeoffs.
[19:00] Arjun Patel: How long to spin up Dedicated for pilot?
[19:05] Jamie Park: Typical lead time is 48–72 hours to provision dedicated pool and run initial benchmarks; can be faster with existing capacity in region.
[19:30] Maya Singh: On the legal/compliance timeline — we need SOC2 docs and SLA templates before we go live.
[19:40] Jamie Park: I'll include SOC2 summary, ISO attestation, and a draft SLA in the security pack.
[20:05] [Slight audio flub, transcription shows 'kubernetes/vpc' as 'coobernates vp c']
[20:25] Sophie Chen: One more thing: we'll also show you how to use the error analyzer to identify prompts that degrade under INT8; it's an automated diff tool.
[20:50] Lena Ortiz: Good. Could you also add per-route dashboards for token-level cost so our Finance team can see spend?
[21:00] Marco Ruiz: Yes, per-route breakdowns are available in the Console; you can export CSVs and hook into cost webhooks.
[21:30] Maya Singh: Regarding fallback, is there an option to fall back to hosted Redwood in case Dedicated goes down?
[21:38] Jamie Park: There's an automatic fallback policy; we can failover to a compatible hosted profile, optionally with an increased cost but better availability.
[22:05] Arjun Patel: About eval automation — will Redwood keep historical metrics? we want to see regressions over time.
[22:12] Sophie Chen: Yes, the Console retains historical eval results and quality baselines; retention depends on your plan but we can provide extended retention for enterprise.
[22:45] [Screen shows CSV export and sample diff]
[23:20] Sophie Chen: Quick note on kernel selection: sometimes the INT8 kernel isn't available for a particular op and we fallback to a slower but precise kernel, that can cause p99 spikes. Optimize flags allow us to prefer stability over raw speed if you prefer.
[24:00] Lena Ortiz: I'd rather prefer consistent latency for SLAs even if median is slightly higher.
[24:08] Marco Ruiz: Then we'd choose conservative kernel selection and maybe FP8 on p99-sensitive routes.
[24:30] Jamie Park: Ok — summarizing pilot plan: we'll run a traffic replay + eval comparison for FP16/FP8/INT8, propose Dedicated sizing, and deliver a report with recommended profile and expected cost savings.
[25:00] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. One more operational question: how are model updates handled? We have weekly model pushes, can Redwood handle rolling updates?
[25:10] Sophie Chen: We support model versioning and rollout policies; you can pin a model for a route, do canaries, and then promote. We also track quality regressions per version.
[25:40] Arjun Patel: Any caveats for running custom tokenizers? we have a byte-level tokenizer that differs slightly.
[25:48] Marco Ruiz: We support custom tokenizers in Dedicated/Private deployments but need to validate huggingface/transformers compatibility; some quant kernels assume standard tokenization for speed heuristics.
[26:20] [Minor cross talk]
[26:45] Sophie Chen: Now I'll walk through a sample pilot report template — section 1: traffic characteristics, section 2: per-profile latency/cost/quality, section 3: recommended rollouts and guardrails.
[27:15] Lena Ortiz: Can you include a sensitivity analysis for traffic spikes? we need to know how profiles behave under sudden load.
[27:25] Sophie Chen: Yes, stress tests and autoscaling behavior will be included. Dedicated supports configurable autoscale policies and burst capacity.
[28:00] Maya Singh: How does cache warming work? if we scale up we sometimes see cold-start latency.
[28:08] Marco Ruiz: We do prefix/KV cache warming strategies and background warmers for common prompts; also we can pre-warm embeddings and common prefixes during deploys.
[28:40] Arjun Patel: On observability, do you expose per-token timing to trace problematic tokens?
[28:48] Sophie Chen: We provide per-token breakout for samples in the debug view, not for every request by default due to cost, but it's available for traces and can be enabled for sampling.
[29:20] [Short pause]
[29:45] Jamie Park: Anything else from ByteWave before we close?
[29:52] Lena Ortiz: Just to confirm, we'll get the security pack, the benchmark CSVs, and a proposed Dedicated sizing doc?
[30:00] Jamie Park: Yes we'll send those. Also will propose pilot dates; suggested window next week if possible.
[30:20] Maya Singh: We prefer later next week after internal alignment; we'll aim for 2026-07-27 to start the replay.
[30:30] Jamie Park: Noted — we'll tentatively block that.
[31:00] Sophie Chen: Quick demo follow-up — I'll attach the exact eval diff examples and the recommended per-layer quant params in the follow-up email.
[31:20] Arjun Patel: One last question — are there regulatory concerns with FP8 on certain chips? we've heard rumors about export control for specific kernels.
[31:30] Marco Ruiz: Not at Redwood's level; hardware vendors sometimes have caveats but for most standard deployment regions it's fine. We'll confirm specifics in the security pack.
[32:00] Lena Ortiz: Ok thanks all.
[32:05] [Small laughs]
[32:20] Jamie Park: To recap next steps: 1) Redwood sends security pack, pricing and a tailored pilot proposal; 2) ByteWave shares sampled traffic traces and eval prompts; 3) Redwood runs benchmark and returns a detailed report and recommendation.
[32:45] Lena Ortiz: Agreed. We'll get the traffic by 2026-07-24.
[33:00] Maya Singh: Also one action — Sophie will send the list of top-10 failure prompts for INT8.
[33:10] Sophie Chen: Yep will attach that.
[33:30] [Wrap-up tone]
[34:00] Jamie Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and Slack.
[34:20] Lena Ortiz: Thank you.
[34:30] [Call ends, recording stops at ~34:40 in system log but duration recorded as 42 mins due to pre/post buffers and a short post-call admin chat that wasn't fully transcribed]

Notes: transcript includes minor transcription errors, e.g., 'coobernates vp c' for 'Kubernetes/VPC'. Attachments referenced: pilot_proposal.xlsx (link), quant_benchmarks_raw.csv (link), security_pack.pdf (link).
